chapter_note.about: This chapter is about what a process is and how the OS creates, stops and restarts many of them. It starts with the process and its control block, the states a process moves through, and how threads differ. Then it covers what a context switch saves and when the CPU changes between user and kernel mode. The second half is fork(): what it returns, how to count the processes it makes, how processes communicate, and how a parent collects a finished child.
chapter_note.simple: A program is a recipe. A process is someone cooking it right now, with their own pot and bookmark. The OS keeps a card for every cook so it can pause one cook, let another cook for a while, and then come back to the first without losing their place. Cooks can have helpers (threads) who share the same kitchen but each keep their own to-do list. A cook can also make a copy of themself with fork(), and then you must count carefully how many cooks there are. In exam words: process, PCB, states, threads, context switch, mode switch, fork(), IPC, wait.

cards.title: Process, program and PCB
cards.simple: A recipe in a cookbook is just words on paper. It does nothing by itself. When someone actually cooks it, that is a process. Two people can cook the same recipe at the same time, and each has their own pot, their own progress and their own bookmark. The OS keeps a small card for each cook with their progress and bookmark. That card is the PCB. In exam words: a program is a passive file; a process is a program in execution; the PCB stores the process state, program counter, registers, page-table pointer and open files.
cards.idea: A **program** is a passive file on disk. A **process** is that program in execution, with its own address space, open files and CPU state. The OS keeps everything it needs to stop and restart a process in a table entry called the **process control block (PCB)**.
cards.definition:
PCB fields: process id (pid), process state, program counter (PC), saved CPU registers, page-table pointer (or memory limits), open-file table, scheduling data and accounting data.

One program can have many processes at once. The program file is shared; the PCB, the address space and the execution state belong to one process only.
cards.intuition_full: The CPU can run only one process at a time per core, but the OS wants to share it among many. To pause one process and later resume it, the OS needs a place to store its state: where it was in the code, what the registers held, where its memory is and which files it has open. The PCB is that place. When a process is switched out, its CPU state is written to its PCB. When it is switched in, the state is read back. The PCB is also how the OS finds everything about a process: the scheduler queues are lists of PCBs. A program itself carries none of this. It is only the code and static data. That is why two users running the same editor create two processes with two PCBs but share one file on disk, and the read-only code pages can even share physical memory.

examples.setup: Two users, A and B, both start the same editor program. Show what the OS creates and what happens to the PCBs when the OS switches from A to B.
steps: A program is a file on disk. It is passive and has no state of its own. Two users, A and B, are about to run the same editor.
User A starts it. The OS creates process 101 and a PCB to hold its pid, state, saved PC and page-table pointer.
User B starts the same program. The OS creates a second process, 102, with its own PCB. One program, two processes.
Process 101 gets the CPU. Its PCB state becomes running and the PC is 0x4A20.
A timer interrupt stops 101. The OS saves its PC (0x4A24) into PCB 101, marks it ready, and runs 102 from its own saved PC (0x4A00).
Each PCB holds its own pid, state, PC and page table. The file is shared; the execution state never is.
examples.answer: One program, two processes, two PCBs. The OS saves and restores PC and registers through the PCBs.

examples.setup: Classify each item as stored in the PCB (per process) or not: (i) the machine code of the program, (ii) the program counter, (iii) the table of open files, (iv) the saved value of register R3, (v) the pointer to the page table. How many belong to the PCB?
steps: (i) The machine code lives in the executable file and in memory pages. It is the program, not per-process state.
(ii) The PC says where this process stopped: PCB.
(iii) Open files belong to the process: PCB (or a table the PCB points to).
(iv) A saved register value is part of the CPU state of the stopped process: PCB.
(v) The page-table pointer says where its memory is: PCB.
examples.answer: 4 items, (ii) to (v). The code is shared by all processes of the program.

examples.setup: Three users run the same program at once. How many programs, processes, PCBs and copies of the code in memory are there?
steps: There is one program file.
Three runs make three processes, so three PCBs.
The code is read-only, so the OS can keep one physical copy of the code pages and map it into all three address spaces. Data and stacks are separate.
examples.answer: 1 program, 3 processes, 3 PCBs, and typically 1 shared copy of the code in memory.

cards.title: Process states
cards.simple: Think of people at a bank. Someone enters (new), takes a ticket and sits in the waiting area (ready), goes to the counter when called (running). If the clerk says 'we need a document from the vault', the customer steps aside and waits for the vault (waiting). When the document arrives, the customer does not jump to the counter. They take a seat in the waiting area again and wait their turn. If the clerk says 'your five minutes are up, go back and wait', the customer returns to the waiting area too. In the end the customer leaves (terminated). In exam words: new, ready, running, waiting, terminated; waiting goes only to ready.
cards.idea: A process is always in one of five **states**: new, ready (waiting for the CPU), running, waiting (blocked on I/O or an event) and terminated. The OS moves it along fixed arrows. **Waiting never goes straight to running**: it must become ready and be dispatched again.
cards.definition:
Legal moves: New $\to$ Ready (admit); Ready $\to$ Running (dispatch); Running $\to$ Ready (preemption, time slice over); Running $\to$ Waiting (blocking call, I/O request); Waiting $\to$ Ready (event or I/O done); Running $\to$ Terminated (exit).

There is no Ready $\to$ Waiting arrow and no Waiting $\to$ Running arrow. Only a running process can block, and only the scheduler can start a ready one.
cards.intuition_full: The states reflect two different shortages. Ready means the process has everything except the CPU. Waiting means it lacks something else, like data from the disk, so giving it the CPU would be pointless. When that missing thing arrives, the process is no longer blocked, but the CPU may be busy, so it joins the ready queue like anyone else. That is why the arrow from Waiting goes to Ready and not to Running. Preemption also leads to Ready, since the process could run again at once if the CPU were free. A running process can leave in three ways: it finishes (Terminated), it is forced off (Ready) or it asks to wait (Waiting). Counting the times a process enters the ready queue is a common exam task. Each blocking call that completes, and each preemption, gives one entry.

examples.setup: A process is admitted, runs, makes one blocking I/O call, runs again, is preempted once, runs again and exits. Follow it through the states, and count how many times it enters the Ready state after its first admission.
steps: A process is created. It is in the New state and is not yet competing for the CPU.
Admit: the OS accepts it. New to Ready. The process waits in the ready queue for the CPU.
Dispatch: the scheduler picks it. Ready to Running.
The process asks for disk I/O, a blocking call. Running to Waiting.
The I/O finishes. Waiting to Ready. It cannot go straight to Running: it has to queue again.
Dispatch again: Ready to Running.
Its time slice ends, so a timer interrupt preempts it. Running to Ready.
Dispatch: Ready to Running.
The process finishes and calls exit. Running to Terminated. Entries into Ready after the first admission: 2.
examples.answer: 2 entries into Ready (one after the I/O, one after the preemption).

examples.setup: A process alone on the CPU has two CPU bursts of 25 ms and 12 ms, separated by one I/O wait. The scheduler uses round robin with a quantum of 10 ms. Excluding its first admission, how many times does it enter the Ready state?
steps: Burst 1 (25 ms): runs 10 ms, preempted (entry 1). Runs 10 ms, preempted (entry 2). Runs the last 5 ms, then blocks for I/O.
The I/O completes: Waiting to Ready (entry 3).
Burst 2 (12 ms): runs 10 ms, preempted (entry 4). Runs 2 ms and exits.
examples.answer: 4 entries into Ready.

examples.setup: Same quantum of 10 ms, but the bursts are 20 ms and 10 ms with one I/O wait between them. How many entries into Ready after the first admission?
steps: Burst 1 (20 ms): the first 10 ms ends the quantum, so it is preempted (entry 1).
The second 10 ms finishes the burst exactly at the end of the quantum. The process then blocks for I/O. It is not preempted, because it asked to wait.
I/O done: Waiting to Ready (entry 2). Burst 2 (10 ms) fits in one quantum and the process exits.
examples.answer: 2 entries. When a burst is an exact multiple of the quantum, the last slice ends in a block, not a preemption.

cards.why: The state diagram is the vocabulary of all scheduling and synchronisation questions. In GATE: which transition is impossible, or how many times a process enters a state.
how: Draw the five states and the six legal arrows.

Count the arrows into the state you are asked about.
Remember: Waiting goes only to Ready.
cards.mistake: Letting Waiting go straight to Running. A process that was blocked becomes ready first. Also, do not count a preemption at the very end of a burst that ends the quantum exactly.
edge_cases: Some systems add suspended states for swapped-out processes; the five-state model is the GATE default.
A process in Ready is not waiting for I/O; it only waits for the CPU.
A running process cannot go directly to New.

Synchronisation chapter: blocked on a semaphore means Waiting.

cards.title: Threads versus processes
cards.simple: A process is like a flat shared by three roommates. They share the kitchen, the fridge and the post box (code, global data, heap and open files). But each roommate has their own bedroom and their own to-do list (a stack, registers and a PC). If one roommate puts milk in the fridge, the others see it. If one roommate writes a private note in their own room, the others cannot read it. In exam words: threads of one process share code, globals, heap and open files; each has its own stack, registers and program counter.
cards.idea: A **process** owns the address space and the resources. Its **threads** run inside it. All threads share the code, the global data, the heap and the open files. Each thread has its own **stack**, **registers** and **program counter**, so that it can be at a different place in the code.
cards.definition:
Per process (shared by its threads): code, global and static data, heap, open files, signal handlers, address space.

Per thread (private): stack, register set, program counter, thread id (and thread-local data).

User-level threads are managed by a library, and the kernel sees one thread, so one blocking system call blocks all of them. Kernel-level threads are scheduled by the OS and can run on several cores.
cards.intuition_full: A thread is a unit of execution, not a unit of ownership. Splitting them lets one program do several things at once without paying the price of a new address space. Creating a thread needs only a stack and a register set. Switching between threads of one process is cheap because the address space stays the same, so no page-table change and no TLB flush is needed. The shared memory is the reason threads are efficient and the reason they need synchronisation: two threads can touch the same global variable at once. The private parts are exactly what lets two threads be at different points of the same code: the stack holds each one's local variables and return addresses, and the PC and registers hold where it is. With kernel threads the OS sees each thread separately, so one can block while others run. With user-level threads the kernel sees a single execution stream.

examples.setup: A process has three threads. List what exists once, and what exists three times. If thread 1 sets a global variable g = 7, who sees it?
steps: A process owns one address space and its resources. Threads will run inside it.
These are shared by all threads: one copy of the code, of the global data, of the heap and of the open files.
Thread 1 is created. To run by itself it needs its own stack and its own registers and PC.
Thread 2 is created: another stack, another set of registers and PC.
Thread 3 is created in the same way. Three threads, three stacks, three PCs.

Shared: 1 code, 1 globals, 1 heap, 1 file table. Private: 3 stacks, 3 register sets. If thread 1 sets the global g = 7, threads 2 and 3 see 7. Thread 1's local variable lives on its stack and they cannot see it.
examples.answer: Once: code, globals, heap, file table. Three times: stack, registers, PC. All threads see g = 7.

examples.setup: A process has three threads on one CPU. T1 needs 2 ms of CPU, then a blocking read of 10 ms, then 3 ms more CPU. T2 and T3 each need 5 ms of CPU. How long does the process take to finish all work with user-level threads, and with kernel-level threads? Start with T1.
steps: User-level: the kernel sees one thread. When T1 makes its blocking read at 2 ms, the whole process blocks for 10 ms. No other thread can run.
Kernel-level: while T1 waits for the disk, the kernel runs T2 and T3 (10 ms of work) on the CPU.
T1 is ready again at 12 ms and finishes its last 3 ms: total $=2+10+3=15$ ms.
examples.answer: 25 ms with user-level threads and 15 ms with kernel-level threads.

examples.setup: Two threads of one process each call malloc(100) on the shared heap. Do they get the same block? Can thread 2 use the block that thread 1 allocated?
steps: The heap is shared, but malloc hands out a different free block to each call: the two blocks are different.
Thread 1's pointer is an address in the shared address space, so thread 2 can use it if it learns the pointer (for example through a global).
The pointer variable itself, if it is a local, sits on thread 1's private stack.
examples.answer: Different blocks, both visible to both threads. A shared heap means shared address space, not one common block.

cards.why: Threads are everywhere in modern systems, and 'what is shared' is a favourite GATE statement. In GATE: choose the shared and private items, or compare user-level and kernel-level threads on blocking and parallelism.
how: Shared: code, globals, heap, open files.
Private: stack, registers, PC.
User-level threads: kernel sees one thread, so one blocking call blocks all.
Kernel-level threads: can run in parallel on several cores and block separately.
cards.mistake: Saying each thread has its own heap or its own open-file table. Only the stack, registers and PC are private. The heap, globals and files are shared.
edge_cases: Thread-local storage gives a private copy of a variable, but it is an explicit exception.
Local variables are private only because they sit on a private stack; their memory is still in the shared address space.
A user-level thread library cannot use several cores unless the kernel gives it several kernel threads.
connections: Sharing memory is why threads need the synchronisation tools of the next chapter (os.sync).
The context switch card (p4) shows why a thread switch is cheaper than a process switch.

check.a: Any three of: code, global data, heap, open files.

check.q: Which part of a thread's state do other threads not see?
check.a: Its stack (local variables), registers and PC.

check.q: A user-level thread calls a blocking read(). What happens to its sibling threads?
check.a: They all block, because the kernel sees one thread.

cards.title: Context switch
cards.simple: You are reading a book and a friend asks you to help with homework. You put in a bookmark and note down where you were, then open your friend's notebook where they left a note too. When you are done, you go back to your own bookmark. Putting away one task and picking up another takes a little time, and during it you do no reading and no homework. That time is the cost. In exam words: a context switch saves the old process's registers and PC in its PCB and loads the new one's. It is pure overhead. A switch between threads of the same process is cheaper because the address space stays the same.
cards.idea: A **context switch** saves the running process's CPU state into its PCB and loads another process's state from its PCB. While it happens, the CPU does no useful work for any process. Switching between processes also changes the address space. Switching between threads of one process does not.
cards.definition:
Saved and restored: PC, stack pointer, general registers, status flags. For a process switch also the page-table base register (and the TLB is flushed or tagged with an address-space id).

Overhead share with quantum $q$ and switch time $s$: useful fraction $=\dfrac{q}{q+s}$ if every slice is followed by a switch.
cards.intuition_full: The CPU has one set of registers, but many processes want to use it. The only way to share it is to copy the registers out to memory when a process leaves and copy another set in when a new process arrives. The PCB is the place for that copy. The OS may also need to change the memory map. A different process has a different page table, so the page-table pointer changes, and cached translations (the TLB) for the old process become wrong. That extra work is why a process switch is more expensive than a thread switch inside one process. The same address space is kept, so the page table and TLB stay valid and only the registers, stack pointer and PC change. A switch is triggered by an interrupt (timer), a blocking call or an exit. It never does useful work for the program, so frequent switches lower the share of time spent on real work.

examples.setup: Process A runs with PC 0x1004, SP 0x7F00 and R1 = 7. Process B is ready, with saved PC 0x2040, SP 0x6F00 and R1 = 3 in its PCB. A timer interrupt fires. Describe the switch from A to B.
steps: Process A is running. The CPU registers hold A's values: PC 0x1004, SP 0x7F00, R1 = 7 and A's page table. Process B, ready, has its saved values in PCB B.
A timer interrupt arrives. The CPU enters kernel mode and the scheduler starts. A's time slice is over.
Save: the OS copies the CPU registers into PCB A: PC, SP, R1 and the page-table pointer.
The scheduler picks B from the ready queue.
Load: the OS copies PCB B into the CPU, including B's page-table pointer. Address translation now follows B's page table, so A's cached TLB entries are useless.
B resumes at PC 0x2040 as if it had never stopped. No useful work was done during the switch itself: it is pure overhead.

cards.title: System calls and mode switch
cards.simple: A shop has a public floor and a staff-only back room. Customers (your program) can walk around the floor freely, count items, and do their own sums. To get something from the back room, they must ring a bell and a staff member goes in for them. Ringing the bell is a system call. The staff member also steps in on their own when something goes wrong, like a spill (a page fault) or a customer asking for the impossible (dividing by zero). Walking around the floor, using a calculator or reading the price list (library functions that stay on the floor) never needs the back room. In exam words: a trap moves the CPU from user mode to kernel mode. System calls, interrupts and exceptions such as page faults cause it. A plain function call does not.
cards.idea: The CPU runs in **user mode** for ordinary code and in **kernel mode** for the OS. A **mode switch** from user to kernel happens on a **trap**: a system call, a hardware interrupt or an exception such as a page fault. Ordinary instructions, function calls and most library functions stay in user mode.
cards.definition:
Causes of a switch to kernel mode: (1) a system call (software trap), for example read, write, sleep, exit, fork; (2) a hardware interrupt, for example a timer or I/O completion; (3) an exception, for example a page fault or division by zero.

No mode switch: arithmetic, calls and returns inside the program, and library functions such as strlen or malloc that do not need the kernel (malloc enters the kernel only when it must ask for more memory).
cards.intuition_full: Kernel mode lets the CPU run privileged instructions that can touch hardware and all of memory. User programs must not do this directly, so the hardware allows entry to the kernel only through controlled doors: the trap instruction and the interrupt and exception vectors. A system call is a request that goes through one of these doors, with the call number and arguments passed in registers. The kernel does the job and then returns to user mode. The cost of a trap is the entry, saving registers, doing the work and returning. That is why programs batch work: one big write is cheaper than many small ones. Library functions are ordinary user code. A function such as printf may call write inside, but only when its buffer needs flushing. So the number of kernel entries can be much smaller than the number of library calls. A mode switch is not the same as a context switch. A mode switch changes privilege on the same process. A context switch changes the process.

examples.setup: A program executes, in order: z = x + y; read(fd,buf,n); strlen(s); sleep(5); f(a) (its own function); a page fault; x / 0. Which events switch the CPU from user mode to kernel mode?
steps: z = x + y is plain arithmetic. It runs in user mode, so there is no mode switch.
read(fd, buf, n) is a system call. It executes a trap instruction, and the CPU enters kernel mode to do the read. Mode switch 1.
strlen(s) is a library function that only reads the program's own memory. After the read returns, the CPU is back in user mode and stays there. No switch.
sleep(5) is a system call: the program must ask the kernel to block it. The CPU traps again. Mode switch 2.
f(a) calls a function inside the program. It is an ordinary jump and return in user mode. No switch.
A page fault is raised by the hardware when the page is not in memory. The CPU traps into the kernel to load it. Mode switch 3.
x / 0 raises a divide-by-zero exception, so the CPU traps into the kernel to handle it. Mode switch 4.
Total: 4 of the 7 events change the mode: read, sleep, the page fault and the divide error. Plain arithmetic, library calls like strlen and the program's own calls do not.

examples.setup: A program makes 1000 system calls per second. Each call costs 2 $\mu$s to enter the kernel, 3 $\mu$s of kernel work and 2 $\mu$s to return. What fraction of the CPU goes to system calls?
steps: Cost of one call $=2+3+2=7\ \mu$s.
Per second $=1000\times7\ \mu\text{s}=7000\ \mu\text{s}=7$ ms.
Fraction $=7\text{ ms}/1000\text{ ms}=0.7\%$.
examples.answer: 0.7% of the CPU.

examples.setup: A program writes 1 MB ($2^{20}$ bytes) to a file using printf. The C library has a 4096-byte buffer and calls write() only when the buffer is full. How many system calls are made? How many would be made if every byte were written with its own write()?

With no buffering: one write() per byte, $2^{20}=1\,048\,576$ calls.
printf is a library call. It enters the kernel only when it flushes.
examples.answer: 256 system calls with buffering against 1 048 576 without. A library call is not necessarily a system call.

cards.title: fork() semantics
cards.simple: Imagine a photocopier that can copy a whole notebook, including the page marker showing where you are. You make a copy and hand it to a friend. Now you both start reading from the same line. But if your friend scribbles in their copy, your copy stays clean. The only difference is that you are told your friend's name, while your friend is told 'you are the copy'. In exam words: fork() creates a child process that is a copy of the parent. It returns the child's pid in the parent, 0 in the child, and each has its own private copy of all variables.
cards.idea: **fork()** creates a new process that is a copy of the caller: same code, same next line, and its own copy of every variable. It returns **twice**. The parent gets the child's pid, and the child gets **0**. After that the two run independently and changes in one do not appear in the other.
cards.definition:
$\text{fork()}=\begin{cases}0 & \text{in the child}\\ \text{child's pid}>0 & \text{in the parent}\\ -1 & \text{on failure}\end{cases}$

Both processes continue from the instruction after fork(). Memory is copied (logically; real systems use copy-on-write), so a variable changed by one is not changed in the other. Open files are shared in the sense that the child inherits the descriptors. Buffered output that has not yet been flushed is copied too.
cards.intuition_full: fork() duplicates the running program at one instant. Everything the parent has is copied: code, global and local variables, the stack, the registers and the position in the code. The only difference is the return value, which is the program's way to know which copy it is. Tests like if (fork() == 0) pick out the child, and else picks out the parent. Because memory is copied, variables are not shared between parent and child. Writing x in the child changes only the child's x. That is the opposite of threads. Real systems delay the physical copy until one of the processes writes (copy-on-write), but the effect is the same. The copy includes everything in the process's memory, such as unflushed output buffers. This explains a classic surprise: text printed with printf before the fork can come out twice if the output is buffered.

steps: One process runs. It has set int x = 7 and reaches the line if (fork() == 0).
fork() creates a child: a copy of the parent with the same code, the same next line and its own copy of x = 7.
fork() returns twice. In the child it returns 0. In the parent it returns the child's pid, here 4321.
Child: the test is true, so x = x * 3 = 21 and it prints 21. Only the child's copy changed. The parent's x is still 7.
Parent: the test is false. wait(NULL) returns once the child has exited. Then x = x + 1 = 8, and it prints 8. Output: 21 8.
examples.answer: The output is 21 8. The child prints 21 and the parent, which waited, prints 8.

steps: First fork: in the parent (fork() is nonzero) i becomes 2. In the child (fork() returns 0) i becomes 3.
Second fork: it runs in both processes, so there are four processes in the end. In each, the parent side adds 4 and the child side adds nothing.
From the process with i = 2: parent side prints 6, child side prints 2.
From the process with i = 3: parent side prints 7, child side prints 3. Four processes print 6, 2, 7 and 3, in any order. The sum is 18.
examples.answer: The four values 2, 3, 6 and 7 are printed in some order. The sum is 18.

steps: printf(A) puts A in the output buffer. The buffer is not flushed, since there is no newline and the output is a file.
fork() copies the whole process, including the buffer. Parent and child both hold A.
Each then adds B to its own buffer. At exit each flushes AB: 4 characters in all.
With unbuffered output, A would be written before the fork and each process would write B: ABB, 3 characters.

cards.title: Counting processes made by fork()
cards.simple: Imagine each person in a room can clone themselves once every time a bell rings. After one bell, 1 person becomes 2. After the second bell, those 2 become 4, because the clone also clones. After three bells there are 8. But if the rule says 'only people wearing a red hat may clone', then only some people double, so you must follow each person to count. In exam words: n unconditional forks in a row give 2^n processes. When a fork is inside a condition, a loop with break, or in a branch that only the child takes, trace which processes reach it.
cards.idea: Every process that reaches an unconditional **fork()** doubles. So $n$ forks in a row give $2^n$ processes, and $2^n-1$ children of the original. If a fork sits inside an **if**, a loop that **breaks**, or a branch that only the child takes, only some processes run it. Then draw the process tree and count.
cards.definition:
Unconditional: processes $=2^n$, children of the original $=2^n-1$.

Conditional: follow each process separately. A process creates a child each time it executes fork(); the child starts after the fork() with return value 0 and continues. The child inherits the loop counter and variables at that moment.

In expressions: $a\ \&\&\ b$ runs $b$ only if $a$ is true; $a\ \|\ b$ runs $b$ only if $a$ is false. Remember that fork() is true (nonzero) in the parent and false (0) in the child.
cards.intuition_full: Each fork() call turns one running process into two at the same point in the code. The child then runs the same code that follows, including later forks. This is why forks in sequence multiply: the child also executes all the forks that come after the one that created it. If a fork is guarded by a condition that depends on the fork's own return value, such as if (fork() == 0), then the condition separates parent and child. Then only one side executes the guarded code. The cleanest method is to draw a tree: each node is a process, each edge a fork it executed. To get the count, ask for each process which forks it reaches. Short-circuit operators decide this automatically. With &&, only the side that got a nonzero value (the parent) goes on. With ||, only the side that got zero (the child) goes on. Also remember that the loop variable is copied: a child created in iteration i continues with i, and may run the remaining iterations.

steps: Start: one process, P.
Line 1, fork(): P creates child a. Two processes.
Line 2, fork(): both P and a execute it. P creates b and a creates c. Four processes.
Line 3, if (fork() == 0): all four processes run the fork. Each makes a new child (d, e, f, g), and in that child fork() returned 0. Eight processes.
Only the four new children pass the test == 0, so only they run the inner fork(): h, i, j and k are created. Twelve processes.
Total: 12 processes, so 11 are children of the original. Check: three unconditional forks give 2^3 = 8, and the inner fork adds one for each of the 4 children that passed the test: 8 + 4 = 12.
examples.answer: 12 processes (11 children of the original).

steps: In each iteration, fork() creates a child. The child (where fork() returned 0) runs fork() once more and then breaks out of the loop.

Everyone leaves the loop and reaches printf: the parent (1), the 4 children (4) and the 4 grandchildren (4).
Total printf calls $=1+4+4=9$.

Unconditional: processes $=2^n$, children of the original $=2^n-1$.

cards.title: Inter-process communication
cards.simple: Two friends in different rooms want to share information. A pipe is like passing notes through a school office: each note goes in a tray, and the office staff hand it on. It always needs a visit to the office. Shared memory is like putting a whiteboard on the wall between the two rooms, so both can read and write on it directly. Hanging the whiteboard takes some effort once, but after that no office visit is needed. In exam words: pipes and message passing go through the kernel on every transfer. Shared memory needs the kernel only for the setup, then is accessed directly, so it is the fastest.
cards.idea: **Inter-process communication (IPC)** lets separate processes exchange data, since their memory is private. A **pipe** is a one-way byte stream through a kernel buffer. **Message passing** sends discrete messages through the kernel, even between machines. **Shared memory** maps one region into both processes. It needs the kernel for setup only, and then every access is a normal memory access.
cards.definition:
Pipe: one-way, byte stream, kernel buffer; each write() and read() is a system call. Two-way talk needs two pipes.

Message passing: send() and receive() through the kernel; works across machines and needs no shared variables.

Shared memory: one setup (create and attach) per process, then ordinary loads and stores. The processes must synchronise themselves, because the kernel does not.
cards.intuition_full: Processes cannot touch each other's memory, by design, so any data exchange has to be arranged by the OS. The two basic designs differ in who is in the loop. In message passing the kernel is a middleman for every transfer. That is safe and simple, and it also scales to different machines, but each message costs system calls and copies. In shared memory the kernel only sets up the mapping. After that, the data moves without the kernel, which makes large or frequent transfers cheap. The price is that the programmer must avoid races, since both processes can write at the same time. A pipe is the simplest message mechanism: a kernel buffer with a write end and a read end. After fork(), the child inherits the pipe's descriptors, so parent and child can use it. A pipe carries bytes in one direction.

examples.setup: A parent sends 5 messages of 100 bytes to its child. Count the system calls needed (a) with a pipe and (b) with shared memory (create once, attach in both processes).
steps: Pipe: one pipe() call makes a buffer inside the kernel that both processes can reach. System calls so far: 1.
Each message: the parent calls write(). This is a system call. The kernel copies 100 bytes into its buffer.
Each message: the child calls read(). Another system call. The kernel copies the bytes out. So 2 system calls per message.
Five messages cost $5\times2=10$ calls, plus the pipe() call: 11 system calls in all.
Shared memory: setup asks the kernel to map one region into both address spaces. That takes shmget, then shmat in the parent and shmat in the child: 3 system calls.

Now the parent stores into the region and the child loads from it with ordinary instructions: 0 system calls per message. Five messages still cost 3 calls (plus some synchronisation so the child does not read too early).
examples.answer: 11 system calls with a pipe, 3 with shared memory.

cards.title: wait(), exit, zombies and orphans
cards.simple: Imagine a student who finishes an exam and hands it in (exit). The school keeps a note of the student's score until the teacher collects it (wait). Until then, the student has left, but their record is still on the list. That is a zombie. Now imagine the teacher leaves the school while the student is still sitting the exam. The school principal (init) takes over as the student's contact. That student is an orphan. In exam words: wait() blocks the parent until a child ends and collects its exit status. A child that has ended but not been waited for is a zombie. A child whose parent has already exited is an orphan and is adopted by init.
cards.idea: When a process ends with **exit**, the kernel frees its memory and files but keeps a small table entry with its exit status. The parent collects it with **wait()**. Until then the child is a **zombie**. If the parent exits first, the running child becomes an **orphan** and the OS hands it to **init**, which waits for it.
cards.definition:
wait(&s): blocks the caller until one of its children ends, stores the exit status in s and returns the child's pid. After that the child's table entry is freed.

Zombie: a process that has terminated but whose parent has not yet called wait(). Orphan: a running process whose parent has terminated; its parent becomes init (pid 1).

If the parent never calls wait(), zombies stay until the parent exits.
cards.intuition_full: A child's exit status is information the parent may want, so the kernel cannot throw it away at once. It keeps a minimal record, and that record is the zombie. The zombie uses no memory or CPU, only a slot in the process table. The slot is released when the parent reads the status with wait(). If the parent is long-running and never waits, zombies pile up and can fill the table. The orphan case is the opposite: the parent has gone, so nobody is left to collect the status. The OS gives the child to init, which calls wait() in a loop, so orphans are cleaned up when they end. wait() is also a synchronisation tool: it makes the parent wait for the child, which fixes the order of their output. Without wait(), the order in which parent and child print is up to the scheduler.

examples.setup: Parent P (pid 500) forks child C (pid 501). C exits with status 3, and later P calls wait(). Then P starts C2 (pid 502) and exits before C2 ends. Follow the process table.
steps: Parent P (pid 500) calls fork(). The child C gets pid 501 and its parent is 500.
C finishes and calls exit(3). The kernel frees its memory and open files but keeps its table entry with the exit status. C is now a zombie.
P is busy and has not called wait(). The zombie stays in the process table and uses up a pid slot.
P calls wait(&s). It gets s = 3 and the return value 501. The kernel removes C's entry: P has reaped its child.
The other case: P starts a child C2 (pid 502) and then exits first. C2 is still running, an orphan. The OS makes init (pid 1) its new parent.
When C2 ends, init calls wait() on it, so no zombie is left behind.
examples.answer: C was a zombie until P called wait(). C2 became an orphan, adopted by init.
